title: How to Subnet: CIDR, Masks and Usable Hosts Made Simple
seoTitle: How to Subnet an IP Address: CIDR & Usable Hosts Explained
excerpt: A simple method for working out networks, broadcast addresses and usable hosts from CIDR notation.
description: Learn to subnet an IPv4 address step by step: CIDR notation, subnet masks, block sizes, network and broadcast addresses and usable hosts, with a worked example.
body:
Subnetting looks hard at first, but most exam questions need only one idea: the block size. Once you can find the block size, the network address, broadcast address and usable hosts follow.

## CIDR notation in one line

An IPv4 address has 32 bits. The number after the slash says how many of those bits belong to the network. In 192.168.10.0/24, the first 24 bits are the network and the last 8 bits are for hosts.

## Usable hosts

The formula is 2 to the power of the host bits, minus 2. You subtract 2 because the first address is the network address and the last is the broadcast address, and neither can be given to a device.

- **/24:** mask 255.255.255.0, 256 addresses, 254 usable hosts
- **/25:** mask 255.255.255.128, 128 addresses, 126 usable hosts
- **/26:** mask 255.255.255.192, 64 addresses, 62 usable hosts
- **/27:** mask 255.255.255.224, 32 addresses, 30 usable hosts
- **/28:** mask 255.255.255.240, 16 addresses, 14 usable hosts
- **/29:** mask 255.255.255.248, 8 addresses, 6 usable hosts
- **/30:** mask 255.255.255.252, 4 addresses, 2 usable hosts (often used for point-to-point links)

## The block size method

The block size is 256 minus the last non-zero number in the mask. For a /26 the mask ends in 192, so the block size is 256 − 192 = 64. Subnets start at every multiple of the block size.

## Worked example: 192.168.10.70/26

- **Block size:** 64, so the subnets start at .0, .64, .128 and .192
- **Network address:** 70 falls between 64 and 128, so the network is 192.168.10.64
- **Broadcast address:** one less than the next subnet, so 192.168.10.127
- **Usable hosts:** 192.168.10.65 to 192.168.10.126, which is 62 hosts

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting to subtract 2 for the network and broadcast addresses
- Counting the block size from the wrong part of the mask
- Mixing up the number of subnets with the number of hosts per subnet

## Practise until it is quick

Work a few by hand, then check your answers with the free [subnet calculator](/tools/subnet-calculator/), which shows the network, broadcast, mask and host range for any address. When you're ready, try subnetting questions in the free [Network+ mock test](/network-plus/mock-test/).
